senderIds.verification: I opened all three cited sources and found one more. (1) In pennywise issue #762 a user submitted four Arabic sample messages from the sender 'BanK-AlAhly', covering card spend, ATM and instant-transfer credit. The message bodies do not name the bank. They do quote a 5-digit hotline that matches NBE's published hotline in NBE's own OTP FAQ and in press coverage. Merged PR #776 / NationalBankOfEgyptParser.kt documents 'Sender: "BanK-AlAhly"'. It matches by uppercasing the sender, removing whitespace, '-' and '_', then checking contains('ALAHLY'). (2) The raw Mahafez data dump has exactly two grouping keys, 'VF-Cash' and 'BanK-AlAhly'. The 21 messages under 'BanK-AlAhly' are all instant-transfer notices (about 14 incoming, 7 outgoing), and none of them names the bank. The GitHub blob view hides that key because it truncates the file, so use the raw URL as evidence. (3) PaySync Gateway gives 'BanK-AlAhly' only as a configuration example for 'Allowed senders' and never maps it to NBE in the text. This is weak and should not count as device evidence. Independent confirmation: a separate payment-bridge project's README (GitHub; owner and repo name withheld) lists the National Bank of Egypt (البنك الأهلي المصري, incoming instant transfers) sender as 'Bank-AlAhly', and its test fixture uses the notification title 'Bank-AlAhly' from Samsung Messages. Note the different capitalization of K. No statement from NBE or a regulator was found, so this cannot be 'official'. Match case-insensitively. The pennywise test sender 'AD-BANK-ALAHLY-S' is an invented DLT-style variant, not evidence. Not to be confused with Al Ahli Bank of Kuwait-Egypt or Saudi SNB 'AlAhli'.

Added by the verifier. A separate payment-bridge project's README lists the NBE incoming instant-transfer sender as 'Bank-AlAhly' (lower-case k), and its test fixture uses that notification title from a Samsung Messages capture. Same ID as 'BanK-AlAhly' under case-insensitive matching. Single source, not cross-checked. The project's owner and repo name are withheld here for privacy; the full URL is in the workflow's verify-result.json.

senderIds.verification: I opened the cited source myself. Ingest.kt does list "KFH Egypt" in DEFAULT_SENDERS, under the comment "Egypt — observed on a device". PR #17 repeats that the Egypt seeds were the only IDs seen on a real device. So the claim is not invented, but there are three problems. (1) The exact spelling of the sender is not established. The same file matches senders after lowercasing and removing spaces, hyphens and underscores (Senders.key), so the seed "KFH Egypt" would also match a real sender of "KFH-Egypt" or "KFHEgypt". The PR #30 fixtures store the source only as the slug "kfh-egypt", and the message bodies say "KFH-Egypt". This project's own egypt-sms-formats.json writes the sender as "KFH-Egypt (as seen)", which contradicts the space form in egypt-banks.json. (2) It rests on one source: a single developer's unpublished device, with no screenshot or raw address shown. (3) I found no independent confirmation. The bank's official SMS Banking page (https://www.eg.kfh.com/sms-banking-2/) describes the alerts but names no sender ID or short code. Searches of news sites, forums and Truecaller-style sources in English and Arabic found nothing. The brand is clearly KFH Egypt, the former Ahli United Bank Egypt (rebranded January 2025), so the sender is plausible. Treat it as a hint: match it after removing spaces and hyphens, and do not hard-code the spaced spelling.

senderIds.verification: I couldn't open the cited page myself. WebFetch got HTTP 403 on every form of the URL: /en/ with and without .html, the Arabic version, and the bare alexbank.com host. The Wayback Machine is blocked for this tool. All the evidence comes through the search index. Seven different queries in English and Arabic all reported this list as coming from the bank's 'Keeping you Safe' page, including queries that did not name the IDs. One of them quoted text that looks verbatim: 'You may receive SMSs from the below official Sender names for ALEXBANK'. An exact-phrase search for part of that sentence did not return the page, though. I found no independent second source: febanks.com/39873, bankygate.com/21500, forums and GitHub parsers name no sender. The claim is very likely true, but no one has looked at the page directly. Keep 'official' only on condition that someone views the page in a normal browser.

Same situation as ALEXBANK. The search-index summaries consistently include 'Alex Bank' (with a space) in the official list, but the page returned 403 and I could not check the exact spelling. 'Alex Bank' is also the name of an unrelated Australian institution. That does not matter here because the source is the Egyptian alexbank.com, but the bank's country must stay attached to this ID. Matching should ignore case and spaces. No independent confirmation.

The search index lists it on the safety page, and the page itself returned 403. The context fits: ALEXPOINTS is the bank's loyalty programme, and its redemption pages say a 6-digit PIN and a confirmation SMS are sent. Those pages do not name the sender, though. These are reward-programme messages, not account-debit alerts, so the parser should not treat them as transactions. No independent confirmation.

The search index reports this name on the safety page, but as written it is 12 characters including the space. A GSM alphanumeric sender ID can be at most 11 characters, so this exact string cannot be what appears on the phone. The real sender is probably 'ABMagnifica' or a cut-off 'AB Magnific'. I searched for 'ABMagnifica' and 'AB-Magnifica' and found nothing. Do not store this exact string for exact matching. Downgrade until a real message shows the displayed form.

The search index reports it on the safety page, and the page returned 403. Its length of 10 characters is valid. It is consistent with the bank's Private customer tier, whose ALEXALERTS bundle is free, but no other page names it as a sender. No independent confirmation.

The Arabic search-index snippet places 4988 under an FAQ about the bank's official communication channels, labelled as the SMS service ('خدمة الرسائل النصية القصيرة: ٤٩٨٨'). It does not clearly say that SMS messages arrive from 4988. It could equally be a number customers send SMS to. A direct search for 'alexbank 4988 SMS' found nothing else. Its role as a sender is not established, and I could not view the page (403).

senderIds.verification: I checked the four cited sources myself, and they are not equally strong. (1) The two mahafez_sms_engine data files are the best evidence. They hold 97 and 80 messages (177 in total, matching the claim) whose _address is exactly 'VF-Cash'. Their fields (_protocol, _service_center, _sub_id, _readable_date, _contact_name and so on) are the ones the SMS Backup & Restore app exports, so they look like real phone exports. The service-center values start with Egypt's +20 code, and most message bodies are in Arabic and name the service itself (transfers in and out, withdrawals, balance checks, promotions). The second file also contains 'BanK-AlAhly', so that file is not Vodafone-only. (2) tidybox Ingest.kt is a separate project with a different owner. It puts 'VF-Cash' in DEFAULT_SENDERS under a comment saying the Egyptian IDs were 'observed on a device', and its PR #30 says the templates came from real device samples. This is the independent second sighting. (3) The paysync-gateway README only uses 'VF-Cash' as an e.g. example of what to set as an allowed sender. That is a setup instruction, not evidence that the ID was seen, and this source should be dropped or marked as an example. (4) Tahweel lists lowercase 'vf-cash' in a variant/guess array and in its test samples, which is not evidence either. Its security doc warns that anyone can send a message under the sender name vf-cash through a bulk SMS gateway, so a matching sender ID alone does not prove a message is real. No Vodafone Egypt or NTRA page I could find names this sender ID, so 'official' is not justified. The four entries in the JSON are the same ID repeated and should be merged into one.
